thread_title: Wasabia japonica aka real wasabi!  How to grow (with pics!)
breadcrumb: Wasabia japonica aka real wasabi!  How to grow (with pics!)

posts.body_html:
Hey Mike,

Such happy plants! What's your soil mix? You adding gypsum?

If you're selling these, what's the price and approximate size?

I found these plants grow well under lights, in the outer zones where it's too dark for Neps. They love the highland Nep. lab and I'm thinking of trying some under LEDs. Since they like the lower light, you get really good coverage with per light. It's either too hot or too cold here, most of the time, to grow Wasabi outdoors. I doubt they'd tolerate mid to upper nineties in the shade (summer), or -5 degrees F, in the winter!

I have a congested Daruma needing division, so I may stick a couple in a cool stream bank on the property, which is deciduous shade-looks perfect. They'd have to be brought indoors before the freezing arrives. I'm wondering if the cool water could help offset the summer heat.

thanks!

Rob

posts.body_html:
Hey Rob,

Under lights is a great idea, especially in a basement where it stays cooler.

Last season, we got to 110F during the day for a few days, and the nights were between 72-74F. However, if that goes on for weeks, I'd guess the plants will get stressed out, and if they aren't already acclimated, they'll likely not make it. During our summers, they don't grow crazy fast like they do in the late fall, winter and early spring. Our summers are usually around 78-100F during the day, but the night temps almost always drop down between 55-65F. Strong, healthy, acclimated Wasabi plants can take the high day temps as long as they're under shade cloth, are always kept healthy, are positioned in full shade, have cool nights, and watered regularly. I have no experience growing them in a cold water stream, but I know you have the intuition to figure it out! Daruma seems to almost stop growth when it warms up here, whereas Mazuma keeps going.

My soil mix is approximately 50% potting soil, 50% high quality sand. No gypsum added. If you're growing in a steam, you'll have to really re-think your medium, my mix doesn't breath well enough for aquatic culture. In Japan, they inject fertilizer into the streams, which isn't a sustainable or ecologically responsible practice. In the wild, wasabi plants are found growing on the banks of the creeks, they aren't really found inside the water unless it's after a rain and the water level has risen.


Both the Mazuma and Daruma divisions available are very healthy and are $25/each. These are established divisions, and they're sent bare root. Most of the big leaves are chopped off, but there'll be plenty of smaller leaves in tact so that it shouldn't skip a beat! It's crazy, some of the divisions have leaves that are almost as big as the mother plant's leaves! Here's a sample of a Mazuma division, they're all near this size:

posts.body_html:
It was surprising to see seed capsules on the Wasabia mazuma mother plant! There's so many bogus wasabi seed listings on the internet and very few pictures of the real deal seeds! Sorry, seeds aren't yet ripe, but I'll take photos of them when they're ready.

It was very surprising to see how many seeds were setting on this plant! It's hard to say if these are self pollinating or cross pollinating, but the clone is likely self compatible. These seed pods aren't yet mature despite the unique dark color of the ovary. The immature seeds taste sweet and spicy, they're really flavorful! trouble is, it'll probably take an hour to dehusk all the pods and get a spoonful, not really worth the effort...

Interestingly, W. japonica 'Daruma' doesn't produce as many seed pods, and only the ones that were cross pollinated by hand seem to be taking, so I think that cultivar may be either less self compatible or requires cross pollination. I'll be sowing the seeds from the cross only:from the very little information available, people make it sound like germinating wasabi seeds is very difficult. We'll see! Photos taken 3/25/18:





The inflorescence forms this long as F stem that runs onto the ground. I hung it up on some cinder blocks so you can see it:



Very normal looking "radish-like" flowers:







running low on wasabi divisions, seems like I can't make anymore until end of this fall(already took as many as possible from the mother plants):

Very cool, Mike! My Daruma never set seed, so it looks like at least some Wasabia are self-sterile. It'd be interesting to select seedlings for your climate.

I got a freeze-drier awhile back. I bet 1/2 inch thick slices of rhizome, freeze-dried, then powdered, would produce a superior "instant Wasabi".

You have the Wasabi green thumb, Mike! Did you try planting the seeds, maybe selecting?

My plants are doing OK outdoors, but it has been 92+ during the day and in the mid to upper 70s at night. So, they're in deep shade. No wilting, but they need more light; time to move them indoors, in a basement under LEDs. At least they're not as fussy as Darlingtonia.

Good thing I didn't try any in/bordering the small creek this year. The flash floods turned it into a raging river; they would have gotten blown downstream to who-knows-where, like about 6 of my Shiitake logs!

posts.body_html: FINALLY! I have a harvestable rhizome or stem! This is what REAL wasabi looks like before it's harvested and grated into wasabi paste. photos taken 10/25/18. I still haven't tried it, waiting for some new growth so that I can add more organic, nutrient rich material to the soil and hopefully increase flavor. small amounts of sulfur are regularly added when I water to increase the "firey" flavor. The top of the rhizome or stem is supposed to be less flavorful than the bottom portion. I tried a raw leaf the other day and it was so hot, it gave me that feeling you get when you eat too many chilis!

posts.body_html:
Nice work there Mike! So, how long has this ready-to-harvest stem taken to grow, the often quoted 2 years?

Now you need a shark skin grater. I double-dog-dare you to take that fresh wasabi and a shark skin grater to a sushi restaurant, sit at the bar, and when your meal arrives, proceed to grate some fresh wasabi! Share it and you might get a lot of free sushi!

If you ever get a quantity and want to preserve some as freeze-dried, let me know. I have a freeze drier and the commercial wasabi I favor has been freeze dried. If it's like horseradish, you slice the stem lengthwise, into 3/8 inch strips, freeze-dry, then powder. I'd store it airtight w/ oxygen absorbers, like I do with all freeze dried food. Most will keep fresh tasting for 20 years.

My plants suffered from the constant rain, slugs and caterpillars. They're recovering, but it's clear they don't like wet leaves 24/7. I use gypsum to provide the sulfur. Are you using straight ag. sulfur powder? Pretty acidic stuff; it gets dusted around my blueberries every year or two.

If a rhizome is supposed to grow below ground, isn't "stem" the correct descriptor? At least on my plants, there's not much underground, besides roots.

posts.body_html:
If it was a triple dog dare, I would have possibly taken the bait, but not sure double dog dare is enough to entice such actions Funny story: at our favorite japanese restaurant, my wife brought in a water bottle for my daughter. The waitress, who by the way is incredibly nice and friendly, reminded us no outside food or drinks!

I've been debating whether or not to bring in some real wasabi on a less busy day and asking the chef if he could serve some up and then he can keep the rest. If this stuff tastes really good, I bet he'll go for it.

thanks for the update on your wasabi plants bogman! Are you noticing which cultivar does better under heat stress, or is there no visible difference?

Under the conditions here, it's the normal 2 years before you get a harvestable product. The plants almost completely stop growing from about May thru October, so I think the only places you can get these to produce in a year are right on the coast or high up in the mountains where it's cool all year round.

Regarding whether it's a rhizome or stem, it's a grey area. Some of the side shoots creep horizontally just below the soil surface like a sarracenia rhizome and form roots, so by definition, those are rhizomes. Others grow vertically (the more normal situation) so I guess in that case it's a stem. I think if I say either rhizome or stem, people understand what part I'm talking about.

Sulfur-wise, yes, it's agricultural sulfur, although I'm not sure enough is being used to drastically affect the pH.

That "water" could have been a nutritional supplement in disguise! LOL! Good grief, even water for a little kid...

Not much difference in heat tolerance between the varieties. Maybe a little more tolerance in the Daruma. The Daruma center stalk died out, probably from all the rain this year. Hey, it's raining now. It rained last night. It'll rain tonight. It's supposed to rain Tuesday….

Anyhoo, the Daruma self-propagated as the main stem died, leaving a bunch of little ones, which I need to separate. I did notice the Mazuma plants (2) lost all new growth in the heat, whereas the Daruma kept the tip growth; it just stalled-out. This was days in the 90s and nights in the 70s-about 80% shade.

I think I'll keep them inside. The outdoors isn't fit for growing anything, except the Chinese Water Chestnuts did great.

posts.body_html: Correction: after tasting the real deal wasabi, I'm not dumping these plants at the local nursery, I'm going to grow them out!  The flavor is AMAZING!!  It's really strong: when I was grating it, the components are volatile and they hurt my eyes much like when you cut an onion!  Similar to horse radish, it has that same peppery bite that goes up your nose if you eat too much at once, followed by a sweetness and incredible depth of flavor that's difficult to describe in words.  It can be made into a dip for french fries, and it's the ultimate flavor component/emulsifier for an olive oil and balsamic vinegar based salad dressing!   Japanese eat it with noodles and sushi/sashimi, but I have tried it on my eggs and some meats and without a doubt, it's a GAME CHANGER!!!    The main issue now is finding enough space to grow out sufficient plants so that it can be a regular part of our diet.  There's also supposedly all these incredible health properties behind it, but I'm taking that with a grain of salt.  The flavor and it's ability to pair with so many different types of food is enough for me to want this stuff all the time!

posts.body_html:
Yes, indeed! That's why I often pocket a bit of the real stuff when we go to a decent sushi place. Unlike Horseradish, it has a fast "punch", but recedes faster with much better flavors following. Very clean tasting.

For maximum flavor, chill the stem just above freezing and allow it to react in the fridge for about 3-5 minutes, in a tightly closed jar. A cold stem may hurt your eyes less while grating, or use a fan. Unfortunately, pungency is lost fairly quickly, though it'll keep longer airtight and on ice. I wrapped cold balls of it in plastic wrap, which seemed to help.

The allyl isothiocyanate really holds better if super cold. The best Horseradish I've made is using ice cubes, instead of water, when putting in the food processor. After sitting about 10 minutes in the fridge, it was blazing! Once the reaction, after maceration, is complete, that's when I add vinegar. Adding vinegar too early kills the reaction. I was surprised how long this home-made Horseradish kept its pungency.

Wasabi that has sat out a bit and lost it's "burn" is still tasty. Horseradish that's weak tastes like pickled turnips!

Fortunately, you can store the un-grated stems in the fridge for a month to two, if kept moist.

Sounds like it's time to dedicate some real estate to your plantation!
